**The Keeper at the End of the Post**

The first letter arrived in November, slipped into the lighthouse mail bag along with the salt-rotted bills and the quarterly ledger from the Harbor Authority. Tomas Vane, keeper for thirty-one years at Carrick Point, turned the envelope over in the cold air of the lamp room.

The postmark was a town he did not know. The return address was a number on a street called Gull Row. And the name inside, in a hand so fine it looked scratched with a needle: *Mara Vane, Gull Row, 14.*

He should have burned it. Old keepers had a superstition about mail from places no ship had ever called. But Tomas was not a superstitious man, and the seal on the letter was one of the official harbor seals, pressed correctly, the tower and the wave both sharp. He opened it on the gallery floor, where the November wind moved the lantern flame into a blue tongue.

*Dear Grandfather,* it began. *I have been trying to write for a long time, and I only just found the courage. I do not know your name. I know your face, though. It is in the photograph on the mantel. I am sorry if it is strange that I write to you before I have met you. I am sorry about everything I am going to ask you to do, and I hope you forgive me for asking.*

Tomas read it four times. He read it again with the lamp behind him, so the words fell in shadows, and again with the lamp beside him, so the words were plain. He sat on the gallery bench until his fingers went white inside his gloves.

By the end of the year, there were two more.

The second described a summer. *I saw you in a photograph at the harbor museum,* Mara wrote, *a man in a white coat with your lamp in the background, and I stood there until my legs went numb. I wanted you to know that the lighthouse is not lonely to you the way the world thinks it is lonely. It is the only room where you are completely finished with being a person, and that is the best there is.*

Tomas, who had never spoken that way, who kept his grief in the lamp log and his thoughts in the tide charts, felt his chest go strangely loose. The third letter asked him a question. *Do you still mend the net for Old Brant? He is not dead yet. He will be dead for a long time. But he will die, and I want you to remember the way he laughed at the gulls so hard he threw up seawater. I want to remember it too.*

It was then that Tomas began to understand.

He sat in the kitchen with the letters spread on the table and read them all the way through, and what he found was not magic. What he found was a girl who had read his life in the same way he had read the sea: by the evidence. A note in his logbook from 1887, where he had written that Old Brant's wife had taken him a hot pie one fog morning and he had laughed until his ribs ached. The name of the ship that had hit the rocks in '79. The year the keeper before him, Halloway, had gone blind in one eye and kept writing the log in his sleep.

Mara had found these things. She had found them in books. Somewhere, in a city he had never heard of, in a house with a street called Gull Row, a girl was piecing him together from scraps.

He wrote a letter back. He had not written a letter to anyone in eleven years, not since Halloway's funeral, and his hand shook so badly the first line came out slanted and the ink blotted. He set the blot and began again.

*Dear Girl,* he wrote. *Your handwriting is like your grandmother's. I know this because I watched her write to the doctor when the baby came, and I have watched you write it on your own. Do not be sorry. There is nothing to forgive. I am not angry. I am only curious.*

He told her about the years. The fog of '83, the night the lens cracked and the supply boat missed by six hours. He told her about Old Brant, and about the gulls, and about the way the sea made a sound like a held breath on the north side of the point in deep winter. He told her he had kept the photographs, all of them, and that the one on the mantel at Gull Row was the one he had taken of himself in the gallery after Halloway's death, when he had gone up alone to the lamp for the last time and looked down at the sea and not seen it as a threat but as a thing that was always going somewhere.

The last letter came in March, after the thaw.

*Grandfather,* it said, *I know I have been strange to you. I know it is strange to me. I am only telling you the truth and I have no better way. I am going to the harbor museum this week. I have the tickets. I want to see the real thing. The lighthouse. The room where you live. I am going to stand in the lamp room and look out the same windows you look out of. And then I will write to you again, and this time I will be in the same place as you, whether you can see me or not.*

Tomas read it twice, then went up to the gallery and stood at the railing where she would stand, and he looked down at the harbor. It was gray and calm. A fishing boat was moving out through the entrance. The light of the lamp made a slow circle of white on the water, and the water took it and carried it and gave it back to him, and it was the same light he had kept for thirty-one years and would keep, for all the years left, and it was not lonely, and it had never been lonely.

He did not know what would happen after that. He was seventy-nine years old, and the lighthouse was being automated in the summer, and he would go down to Gull Row and live in a small house and grow old in the same town where his blood line was already waiting for him in a museum and a photograph and a mantel. He did not know what he would do with the letters.

But he kept them. He put them in a tin box under his pillow, in the place where he kept the last of the good tea and the key to the lamp room, and he wrote to her again every month, in a hand that grew steadier with each passing season, telling her about the gulls, and the weather, and the years.

And every year, in March, when the thaw came and the harbor was calm, a letter would arrive on Gull Row, and the girl who had not yet been born would open it, and would read it, and would write back, and the lighthouse would keep turning, and the light would go out into the sea, and the sea would take it, and the world would go on.

But for a little while, on that night in March, the keeper and the girl stood in the same room, on the same balcony, looking out at the same gray harbor, and they did not need to say anything, because they already knew everything.

The first letter arrived on a Tuesday in March, when the fog had been rolling in off the Sound so thick that the beam could be seen only from the lamp room, a pale wound in the gray.

Elias Vane had been keeper of Gull Rock Light for nineteen years by then, and the postboat made its run every Thursday and every Sunday, never on a Tuesday. The letter was on good paper, watermarked with a crest he did not know, and the return address was a house in Portland, Maine, three miles down the harbor from the one he had left when he was a boy. The handwriting was small and slanting, with a flourish on the g's that reminded him, with no logic he could name, of his mother's.

*Dear Mr. Vane,*

*I am writing because I am afraid, and because no one else can tell you. The storm is coming up the bay on the eighteenth, and you must not trust the glass. The needle will lie to you, and the barometer will not. Trust me. — E.V.*

Elias turned the letter over. No postmark. No clerk's stamp from the boat. He put it in his coat pocket and walked the gallery in the rain, watching the sea throw itself at the rocks with the patience of something that had been waiting a long time.

By Friday the second letter came. This one was from a woman's hand.

*My name is Eleanor. I am nine years old, and I live in the house on the corner of Harbor and Marsh, in a room with a window that looks at the church steeple. I have just learned to read, and I am not very good at it, so I have written this letter many times. I love you even though I have not met you yet. Please write back. The boy in the next house is teasing me and I have no one to tell.*

Elias read it three times. Then he sat down at the desk in the keeper's house and opened his logbook, where for nineteen years he had recorded the sea state, the oil gauge, the condition of the wick. That afternoon he wrote:

*My dear girl, I have read your letter four times and I am not frightened. I am only tired. I have a cat and a lamp and the whole of the dark ocean between me and a house on a corner in Portland. I do not know how I am going to answer you. But I will try. Tell the boy on the next house that a gull once stole the whole of the cheese from the larder and we still do not know how it got in there. — E.V.*

He did not know what he meant when he said it, but he meant it.

The letters kept coming, now with a regularity that was worse than the irregularity. Three a week, four, five on the bad weeks. They came from a boy named Samuel who wrote in a cramped hand and asked questions about the tides and the birds that nested under the roof of the lamp room. They came from a girl named Nora who wrote about her cat and about the winter when the river froze solid and she had seen her own breath and thought, *I could go out there and stand on my own breath and it would hold.* They came from Eleanor, who grew taller in the letters, her letters, her handwriting, who in one wrote that she had a scar on her knee from the church steps and asked if the lighthouse cat got cold in winter. They came from a girl who wrote that she was eleven and that she was in love with a boy who played fiddle badly and that she did not know how to say this to her mother.

Elias answered all of them. He learned, without being told, that Eleanor's mother had died when she was six, and that the boy on the next house had moved away, and that Samuel had a sister who was very small and cried at the sound of thunder. He learned the names of the street, the church, the butcher's shop. He learned to write a boy's letter and a girl's letter and a mother's letter, though no mother wrote to him, and he understood, in time, that this was not an absence but a kind of protection.

He began to change. This is the part of the story I want to tell honestly, because the change is not romantic. He stopped drinking the rye he had been drinking for six years. He mended the gallery railing himself. He oiled the lamp at midnight the way his father had taught him, and he spoke to the cat, and the cat, who had his whole life been a creature of pure contempt, began to sit on the step of the door. He wrote letters to people he had not spoken to in years, and the letters, sent to a house in Portland that was a house, were answered, and the people who answered were alive and ordinary and glad he was alive.

The storm came on the eighteenth, as the first letter had said. It rose up the bay with the sky the color of a bruise, and the barometer, which Elias had trusted longer than his own mother, dropped a quarter of an inch in the night and then began to rise again, telling him the storm was breaking. The needle on the compass swayed. Elias stood in the lamp room in the howl and thought, *the glass lies.* He did not trust it. He did what his father would have done: he trimmed the wick, he checked the oil, he polished the lens, and he let the light do its work. It worked. The light turned and turned and the ships found the channel.

But here is what I need you to know, because it is the whole story: the storm did not break, and Elias Vane did not go on the rocks, and no ship was lost that winter. The letters kept coming. Eleanor wrote to say she had not been afraid of the storm, that she had been afraid of being alone in it, and that her grandmother had come from the city and that the grandmother was a woman who kept a garden of tomatoes and said *a house is a house because someone is always about to come home.*

The letters stopped in the spring, the year Elias was fifty-three. One morning there was no letter in the box. The next morning, none. He waited, the way you wait for a tide that will not turn, and he did not know if he was grieving or relieved. Then, in the second week of April, a woman came up the causeway on a Sunday when the boat had run, and she was small and gray-haired, and she stood at the gate of the lighthouse house and said, *I was Eleanor. I have come to say that the letters stopped because my grandmother took over the writing, and I would like to show you the house if you would come down with me.*

Elias walked to her. He had walked to a hundred people in his life, and none of them had ever walked to him. He said, *I would like to see the house.*

They went down to Portland. The house was on the corner of Harbor and Marsh. It was smaller than he had imagined it from the letters, and it smelled of tomatoes and cat fur and the particular smell of a family that had been living in one room at a time for a long time. Eleanor's grandmother had a garden of tomatoes, and she was a woman of such ferocity that Elias, who had stood on a rock in the dark for twenty years and never once feared the sea, felt for a moment that the woman might have swamped the lighthouse by accident if she had walked in the wrong direction. She put him in a chair and she poured him tea and she told him about the boy in the next house, and the girl named Nora, and the cat, and the scar on Eleanor's knee, and she told him all of it in the flat, matter-of-fact tone of someone who has been carrying a long list and is now, at last, setting it down.

Eleanor was not nine. She was forty-eight. She sat across from him and she had his mother's eyes, which was, Elias thought, the most extraordinary thing in the whole world, because he had left that house a boy and the eyes had left with her, and he had spent twenty years thinking they were gone, and here they were, at the table, older and softer and the same.

*You wrote to me,* she said. *You wrote to all of them. I found them after grandmother died. I found them in the attic, in a box labeled "For Eleanor." I thought you were mad, and then I thought you were not, and then I did not know what to do with it. So I did nothing. And then I thought, you have been writing for twenty years, and you have been waiting, and I have been here, and we have been on the same side of the sea, and you have been keeping a light for people who are not on the rock, and I think, and I am not saying this to be unkind, I think you have been waiting for me.*

Elias said nothing for a long time. The tea went cold. He said, *I was keeping the light for the ships. That was the work.*

*And the letters,* she said.

*The letters were the work. The light was the work. I did not know the difference for a while. And then I did.*

Eleanor's grandmother was alive at the end of that day, and the tomatoes were in the ground, and the cat, which was old and grumpy and had outlived three lighthouse keepers, was sleeping on a cushion by the stove. Elias sat in the chair and he drank the cold tea and he thought about the fog on a Tuesday in March, and about a boy's flourish on a g, and about the boy who stole the cheese from the larder, and he thought, *I am not a ghost, and I am not a dream, and I am a man on a rock who wrote a letter to a girl who did not exist yet and lived, for a while, as if the future were a room he could walk into and sit in and be given a chair.*

He did not go back to the lighthouse. He stayed in Portland for the spring. He walked to the corner of Harbor and Marsh, and he stood there for a long time, and the church steeple stood there, and the window looked up at the sky, and he thought, *someone is always about to come home,* and he went to the butcher's shop, and he bought a piece of fish, and he went to the harbor, and he watched the water, and the water was gray and the light was on, and he was not on the rock, and the light was not on him, and the light was on the ships, and the ships were coming in, and he was alive, and the cat was sleeping, and the tomatoes were growing, and he had written a letter to a girl who did not exist yet, and she had come back and sat across from him and said *you have been waiting,* and he said, *yes, I have been waiting,* and it was the truest thing he had ever said, and the truest thing he had ever been.

He said it was a place where he belonged. The sea was his wife. The wind was his child. The light was the only prayer he had left.

# The Last Light

The first letter arrived in the hold of the supply boat in April, 1963, wrapped in oilcloth, as if it had been carried in from a drowned house. The postmark read Lumen Point. Elias Wren, keeper of Black Rock Light, turned the envelope over in the lamplight. He had kept the light for thirty-one years. He knew every cove and headland within a day's sail of the point. Lumen Point was not among them.

The letter was a single sheet of blue paper, written in a hand that slanted to the right, as if the writer were hurrying.

"Dear Keeper. I don't know how this is reaching you, or how long it has been waiting on the boat. My name is Mara. I am writing to the man on the point because I have been told he is still there. I have been told you keep your tea in a tin can and you hum off-key when the fog comes in. I don't know if any of this is true. I'm writing because someone has to."

Elias set the letter down. Outside, the point lay white and patient under the morning. He kept a tin of black tea on the shelf. He hummed when the fog came. He had never written a letter in his life, and he had no particular reason to start.

He told no one. Not to the boat's captain, who brought the mail and said nothing. Not to the woman at the harbor store in the village below. A keeper's business was the light, the weather, the log. Everything else could be set aside.

He put the letter in the box on the shelf and went back to his rounds.

---

By June there had been eleven letters.

Mara wrote of a town called Lumen Point: a small harbor town with a bakery that put salt in the crust of the rye bread, a school with a bell that cracked on the third strike, and a dog named Biscuit that sat outside the bakery and barked at boats. She wrote of the storm in November and the one after it in March. She wrote of her life the way one writes of a room one has lived in: the cracks in the windowpane, the stain on the table, the window that stuck and had to be pushed with both hands.

She wrote of a woman who had kept the story of Black Rock alive for forty years, and of a promise made at her deathbed, which was to write to the lighthouse. She wrote: *I have made the promise. I am keeping it. If the lighthouse is still there, then someone is still there to read it. I am writing to that someone.*

And then she wrote the things that could not be known. The step on the gallery that had worn a groove on the left edge from decades of boots. The way the fog chamber smelled of hot iron and kerosene. The way the horn's tone was not a true B but a little lower, as if it had been tuned down so as not to wake the fishermen. She wrote of the keeper's chair and said: *It sags on the east side. I have seen it once, in a photograph. The chair is still there.*

The dates were strange. Lumen Point, 2052. The postmark was clean, the ink black, the paper dry. No damp. No sea. It had not been through water.

Elias began to keep them. He put them in a box on the shelf, and he wrote the dates in his logbook beside the weather. On the day of the November storm, the log read: *Wind from the northwest, sixty knots, light intact. The woman on the sea says the storm was bad. It was.*

He wrote back. Not knowing where to send it, but into the outgoing mail of the supply boat, in the sack with the salt and the candles. He wrote, very short:

"Dear Mara. The step is on the right, not the left. I'm correcting the record. The tea is black. I'm sorry I don't know what you mean by 'the last keeper.' I am only a man who kept the light."

He did not feel pride. He did not feel anything that could be named. He only put the tin of tea where it always was, and went to check the lamp.

---

Mara's next letter came a month later, and it was longer than any of the others.

"Your step is on the right. I was wrong. I am sorry. I have been wrong about things. I am not your granddaughter. I am not your daughter. I am not your sister. I am a woman who was given the light, and I don't know why. My grandmother told me the keeper's name was a secret, and I have spent six years learning it from the logbook. I know now."

Elias read it twice, and set it down, and went outside to stand on the point. The sea was grey, and the light was turning above him.

The next letter: "My name is Elias. I have put it in the logbook. If it is wrong, I am sorry. If it is right, I am glad. I don't know why you wrote it. I don't know why I wrote back. I know that I am still here. I keep the log. I keep the tea. I hum when the fog comes. If that is all I am to you, I don't know what to say. I'm a good man, but I'm not a lot."

The reply: "That's enough. That's all I ever wanted to know. I have stood in your lamp room. The glass is warm. I put my hand on it and I know you were there. You were there, Elias. You kept the light."

He read that letter in the morning, before the coffee. He stood by the window and looked at the sea until the sun came up over the water, and then he made the coffee and the tea, and he put the letter in the box.

He wrote back: "I am not famous. I am just a man who kept the light. If that's what you need, I'll keep it. I'll keep it as long as I can."

She answered: "That's all the fame I ever wanted."

---

By winter, Elias had begun to speak to the letters. He sat in the chair with the letter on his lap and read them aloud. He read them to the lamp, and to the foghorn, and to the sea. He had not spoken to another living person in three weeks. The letters were not living. They were paper and ink and a woman's hand. But they were not nothing.

He wrote a longer letter than he had ever written. He wrote about the storm of '62. He wrote about the night the lamp went out and he had to relight it by hand in the dark. He wrote about his wife, and how the house was quiet, and how he had kept the light because the light needed keeping, and that had been enough. He did not say the last part. He wrote only: *The light needs keeping. I've kept it. I think it's all there is to a man's life, really. To keep something that is not yours.*

The reply came in February. It was short.

"Thank you," she wrote. "I read it. I read it three times. I don't know how to answer something like this. I only know that I am glad. I'm glad you're still there."

He put the letter in the box. He made the tea. He went outside and stood on the point and looked at the light turning in the dark, and he thought: *Somewhere out there, there is a woman who knows the shape of my life. Somewhere out there, there is a bench with my name on it.*

He did not know what that meant. He did not ask. He did not need to.

---

In the spring, the notice came from the Board.

The light at Black Rock would be automated. The date was the last day of October. Elias read the notice three times and put it in his coat pocket and went back to the lamp room. He did not argue. He did not appeal. He had been a keeper for thirty-one years. He knew what the sea was, and he knew that the sea did not ask.

The last letter came with the supply boat on the 28th. It was postmarked Lumen Point, dated the 31st, and it was shorter than any of the others.

"I'm coming tomorrow," it said. "I've never been on the point. I'm going to stand in the chair and hold the lens. I'm going to bring a cup of your tea. I don't know if you'll be there. I don't know if it matters. I'm going because I promised I would be."

Elias read it twice. He set it down. He went to the window and looked at the sea.

He made two cups of tea. He set them on the table by the lamp. He put the blue paper in his pocket. He went to the lamp room, and he polished the brass until it shone, and he climbed the gallery and stood in the chair and looked at the sea.

The 31st of October came. The wind was from the west, and the sea was high, and the fog came in at four in the afternoon and did not lift. Elias stood in the lamp room and turned the light by hand, and he turned it all the way through the night, and he did not sleep.

In the morning, the new mechanism took over. The light turned by itself. It was a clean thing. It was a cold thing. Elias stood in the chair and watched it turn, and he put his hand on the glass, and he felt the warmth.

He wrote in the logbook: *Light extinguished. Keeper present. All well.*

---

In the spring, the supply boat brought one more letter.

It was postmarked Lumen Point. It was dated a week ago. It said:

"I was at your point this winter. I stood in the chair. The chair is cold. But the glass is warm. Someone kept the light a long time before I came. Thank you, Elias. I have kept your name. I will keep it."

Elias read it once, and then again, and then he put it in the box. He made the tea. He set two cups on the table. He went outside and stood on the point, and he looked at the sea, and he listened to the light turning in the dark.

He did not say a word. He did not need to. He had been talking to the sea for thirty years, and the sea had not spoken back. But something had. Something had written to him across the water, across the years, across the whole long dark between one life and the next.

He hummed, off-key, and he turned the light.

She wrote of her grandmother, who had kept the story of the lighthouse alive for forty years, and of a promise made at her deathbed, to write to the last keeper. "I have made the promise," she wrote. "I am keeping it. If the lighthouse is still there, then someone is still there to read it."

And then she wrote the things that could not be known. The step on the gallery that had worn a groove in the left edge from decades of boots. The way the fog chamber smelled of hot iron and kerosene. The way the horn was not a true B but a little lower, as if it had been tuned down so as not to wake the fishermen. She wrote of the keeper's chair: "It sags on the east side. I have seen it once, in a photograph. The chair is still there."

The dates were strange. Lumen Point, 2052. The postmark was clean. The ink was black. The paper was dry. No damp. No sea. It had not been through the water.

Elias began to keep them. He put them in a box on the shelf and wrote the dates in his logbook beside the weather. On the day of the November storm, the log read: "Wind from the northwest, sixty knots, light intact. The woman on the sea says the storm was bad. It was."

He wrote back. Not knowing where to send it, but into the outgoing mail of the supply boat, in the sack with the salt and the candles. He wrote: "Dear Mara. The step is on the right, not the left. I am correcting the record. The tea is black. I don't know what you mean by 'the last keeper.' I am only a man who kept the light."

He did not feel proud. He only put the tin of tea where it always was and went to check the lamp.

Mara's next letter was longer. "I was wrong. I am sorry. I am not your granddaughter. I am not your daughter. I am a woman who was given the light, and I don't know why. My grandmother told me the keeper's name was a secret. I have spent six years learning it from the logbook. I know now. Elias."

Elias read it twice and set it down and went outside to stand on the point. The sea was grey. The light was turning above him.

The next letter: "I know your name. I have put it in the logbook. If it is wrong, I am sorry. If it is right, I am glad." Her reply a month later: "I have stood in your lamp room. The glass is warm. I put my hand on it and I know you were there. You were there, Elias. You kept the light. There is a bench outside the museum with the keeper's name on it. I don't know if it is yours yet. I am going to find out."

He read that in the morning, before the coffee, and he stood by the window until the sun came up over the water. Then he made the coffee and the tea and put the letter in the box.

He wrote: "I am not famous. I am only a man who kept the light. If that is what you need, I will keep it. I will keep it as long as I can." She answered: "That is all the fame I ever wanted."

By winter, Elias had begun to speak to the letters. He sat in the chair with a letter on his lap and read them aloud, to the lamp and the foghorn and the sea. He had not spoken to another living person in three weeks. The letters were not living. They were paper and ink and a woman's hand. But they were not nothing.

He wrote a longer letter than he had ever written. He wrote about the storm of '62, and the night the lamp went out and he had climbed the tower in the dark with a lantern. He wrote about the years when the light had been the only sound in the house, and about how quiet the house had been since his wife died. "The light needs keeping," he wrote. "I think that is all there is to a man's life, really. To keep something that is not yours."

The reply came in February. It was short. "Thank you," she wrote. "I read it three times. I don't know how to answer something like this. I only know that I am glad. I am glad you are still there."

He put the letter in the box and went outside and looked at the light turning in the dark. Somewhere out there, she had said, there was a bench outside the museum with the keeper's name on it. He did not know what that meant. He did not ask.

In the spring, the notice came from the Board. The light at Black Rock would be automated. The date was the last day of October. Elias read it three times and put it in his coat pocket and went back to the lamp room. He had not expected it. The light had not asked to be kept forever. He did not argue. He had been a keeper for thirty-one years. He knew that the sea did not ask.

The last letter came with the supply boat on the twenty-eighth. It was postmarked Lumen Point and dated the thirty-first. "I am coming tomorrow," it said. "I have never been on the point. I am going to stand in the chair and hold the lens. I am going to bring a cup of your tea. I don't know if you will be there. I am going because I promised I would be."

Elias read it twice and set it down and went to the window. He made two cups of tea and set them on the table by the lamp. He polished the brass until it shone, and he climbed the gallery and stood in the chair and looked out at the sea.

The thirty-first of October came. The wind was from the west and the fog did not lift. Elias stood in the lamp room and turned the light by hand all the way through the night, and he did not sleep. He counted the turns. One hundred and twelve turns carried the light once around the world, and he counted every one. In the morning, the new mechanism took over. The light turned by itself. It was a clean thing. It was a cold thing. Elias stood in the chair and watched it turn and put his hand on the glass, and he felt the warmth.

He wrote in the logbook: "Light extinguished. Keeper present. All well."

In the spring, the supply boat brought one more letter. It was postmarked Lumen Point. "I was at your point this winter," it said. "I stood in the chair. The chair is cold. But the glass is warm. Someone kept the light a long time before I came. Thank you, Elias. I have kept your name. I will keep it."

Elias read it once, and then again, and then he put it in the box. He made the tea. He set two cups on the table. He went outside and stood on the point and looked out at the sea and listened to the light turning in the dark. He left the door unlocked. He hummed, off-key, and he turned the light.
